name: neonatal onset multisystem inflammatory disease
aliases: chronic infantile neurological cutaneous and articular syndrome

clinicalPearls: Most severe phenotype of the cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome spectrum, caused by gain-of-function NLRP3 variants that are frequently de novo and often present as somatic mosaicism.
Presents in the neonatal period with a near-continuous migratory urticarial rash, in contrast to the episodic attacks of the milder phenotypes.
Chronic aseptic meningitis produces raised intracranial pressure, chronic headache, papilloedema, optic atrophy, sensorineural hearing loss and, if untreated, developmental delay.
A characteristic deforming arthropathy with bony overgrowth of the epiphyses, especially of the patella and long-bone growth plates, is highly suggestive and can be radiographically distinctive.
Dysmorphic features evolve, including frontal bossing, saddle-shaped nose and macrocephaly, together with growth failure.
Reactive AA amyloidosis is a serious late complication of poorly controlled disease.
Early interleukin-1 blockade transforms the natural history and can prevent irreversible neurological, ophthalmological and auditory damage.
Cerebrospinal fluid typically shows a raised opening pressure with a sterile neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Highly activating NLRP3 variants cause near-constitutive assembly of the cryopyrin inflammasome with minimal need for any trigger, driving continuous caspase-1 activation and overwhelming secretion of interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18. The resulting unremitting innate immune activation produces persistent multisystem inflammation: neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis, chronic aseptic leptomeningitis with raised intracranial pressure, cochlear and optic nerve damage, and a growth-plate arthropathy with disordered endochondral ossification and epiphyseal overgrowth. Somatic mosaicism, in which the activating variant is present in only a proportion of cells, is common and can yield a negative conventional germline test despite classic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Deficiency of the interleukin-1 receptor antagonist
Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis of very early onset
Neonatal sepsis or congenital bacterial meningitis
additionalInvestigations: NLRP3 gene analysis with deep or next-generation sequencing to detect somatic mosaicism
Cerebrospinal fluid examination for raised opening pressure and sterile pleocytosis
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain for leptomeningeal enhancement and ventricular changes
Pure-tone audiometry and serial ophthalmological assessment including fundoscopy for papilloedema
Skeletal radiographs demonstrating epiphyseal and physeal overgrowth
Acute-phase reactants with serum amyloid A and urinalysis for amyloidosis surveillance
redFlags: Signs of raised intracranial pressure such as papilloedema, bulging fontanelle or persistent vomiting
Progressive visual or hearing loss indicating ongoing neurosensory damage
reference.prognosis: Without treatment the disorder causes progressive neurological, visual and auditory disability, deforming arthropathy and a shortened lifespan. Early interleukin-1 blockade substantially improves outcome and can preserve neurosensory function, though damage sustained before treatment is often irreversible.
pitfalls: Concluding the diagnosis is excluded by a negative germline NLRP3 test when somatic mosaicism has not been sought
Misinterpreting the sterile neutrophilic cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis as bacterial meningitis
Delaying interleukin-1 blockade and allowing irreversible neurosensory injury to accumulate
Overlooking the diagnostic value of the characteristic epiphyseal bony overgrowth on imaging
references: Textbook of Pediatric Rheumatology, Cassidy (current edition)
SHARE recommendations for the management of autoinflammatory diseases
